definition.text: Best–worst scaling is a survey choice method in which respondents pick the best and the worst item from a subset of a longer list.

facts.text: Jordan Louviere invented it in 1987 at the University of Alberta, as a form of choice modelling or discrete choice experiment.
The task is repeated with subsets varied by a statistical design, and choices are usually analysed with a random utility model.
Because respondents choose rather than rate, it avoids scale-use bias and stops every item being rated 'quite important'.
It is hard to know how to combine best and worst answers when people use different decision rules for each.

title: Cheap talk

definition.text: In game theory, cheap talk is costless communication between players whose messages do not directly change the game's payoffs.

facts.text: Cheap talk is non-binding and cannot be verified by a third party, so a speaker could lie freely but may choose not to.
It differs from signalling, where sending some messages can be costly for the sender.
In a coordination game a round of cheap talk can help players reach better outcomes, but in the Prisoner's Dilemma it is ignored.

notes: The page covers only the game-theory sense; nothing in the dossier links it to cheap-talk scripts used against hypothetical bias in stated-preference surveys, the likely reason it was seeded here.
